overview: Magadha, centered in present-day Bihar, grew from a powerful kingdom into the heartland of the Mauryan Empire. This map’s approximately 500 to 300 BCE window spans changing rulers and capitals, rather than one unchanging dynasty.

periods.title: Kings around Rajgir
periods.summary: Bimbisara and Ajatasattu belong to the early expansion of Magadha; Rajagaha, modern Rajgir, was its hill-enclosed capital. These phase boundaries are approximate.

periods.title: Toward a wider kingdom
periods.summary: Later rulers, including Mahapadma Nanda, extended Magadhan power. Pataliputra became the capital beside the Ganga; the outline is not an exact record of each conquest.

periods.title: The Mauryan transition
periods.summary: Chandragupta replaced the last Nanda around 321 BCE. The imported Magadha label continues into the beginning of Mauryan rule.

items.text: The 400 to 323 BCE map includes two tiny stray shapes near 65 degrees north in northern Europe. Those are data errors, not Magadhan territories. Even the main Indian outlines should be read as broad historical approximations, not surveyed borders.

Kings could draw on fertile farmland, nearby iron resources, forest elephants and the Ganga’s transport routes. Feeding people, moving supplies and making tools helped build power just as surely as winning battles. Elephants were impressive, but they also needed a great deal of feeding.

Rajagaha stood among hills; Pataliputra, now Patna, commanded routes along the Ganga. Moving the political center changed what a capital could connect: a protected inland setting gave way to a major river junction in the kingdom’s expanding network.

Bimbisara and Ajatasattu pursued conquest, and Mahapadma Nanda later extended the kingdom’s reach. This was a sequence of rulers and expansion, not a single emperor reigning through the whole two-century map window.

Rajgir’s great stone constructions were assembled from boulders without mortar. The Archaeological Survey of India assigns the old and new cyclopean walls to the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. Fitting heavy stones together was an engineering task long before modern cement mixers.

What looks like one enormous defensive wall may have had several jobs. Robert Harding’s 2003 field survey found disconnected stretches and argued that some sections worked as walkways, particularly in later use. Archaeologists test a wall’s function instead of letting its dramatic appearance settle the question.

A memorable name is not always a reliable date. Harding identified the remains called Bimbisara’s Jail as a monastic site of the first millennium CE, centuries after Bimbisara. That label alone cannot identify a cell from the king’s lifetime.

Pottery helps recover the city beneath its religious landmarks. Harding reported Northern Black Polished Ware and associated pre-Mauryan material in the valley, including material in the Inner Fortification. Such finds support early occupation even while the sequence of Old and New Rajgir remains debated.

Across the mahajanapada world, iron ploughshares helped turn heavy soils, while rice seedlings could be raised first and then transplanted into fields. More surviving plants meant more grain. That improvement depended on people doing the painstaking fieldwork, not on a royal command making rice grow by itself.

Large armies and forts needed regular resources. The period’s taxation drew on crops, crafts, trade, animals and forest produce. A kingdom’s strength therefore rested on farmers and workers as well as soldiers, and payment did not always mean handing over coins.

Forests supplied more than elephants: timber was useful for houses, carts and chariots. Rivers supplied water and transport. Ordinary building, carrying and repair connected households to the same landscape that supported the king’s army.

Magadha-Maurya punch-marked coins carried five symbols struck with separate punches, with a karshapana weight standard around 3.4 grams. Making money was literally a series of small hammering jobs. The resulting marks helped distinguish coin types without a modern printed denomination.

Those coins do not normally announce a ruler’s name. The module’s broad fourth to second century BCE dating covers both pre-Mauryan Magadha and Mauryan issues. Scholars compare combinations of symbols and other evidence; a coin cannot simply introduce itself as belonging to a particular king.

A 2024 study used X-rays to examine nine punch-marked coins in the Numismatic Society of India collection at Banaras Hindu University. Silver dominated their metal composition. The specimens span several centuries, and their exact findspots are unknown: useful laboratory evidence, with a real limit on what it can locate.

A Buddhist dialogue set near Rajagaha lists cooks, barbers, weavers, basket makers and accountants. Their earnings support parents, spouses, children and friends. The text imagines a busy economy sustained by skilled work, not only palace servants.

Advice to the young householder Sigala in Rajagaha pairs children’s support for parents with parents’ duty to teach a profession. Teachers should help pupils understand their lessons. These are Buddhist ideals for relationships, rather than proof that every child attended school.

The physician Jivaka’s story begins at Rajagaha and sends him to Taxila for seven years of training. His teacher asks him to find a plant without medicinal use. It is a memorable literary test of knowledge, not a modern claim that every plant is a safe remedy.

Buddhist monastic teaching made nursing a shared responsibility. In a story about a monk with dysentery, the Buddha and Ananda wash him and lift him onto a bed. Good care includes cleaning bodily waste and comforting patients: compassion sometimes involves the least glamorous jobs.

In the Samannaphala dialogue, Ajatasattu’s ministers recommend different religious teachers before the king visits the Buddha in Jivaka’s mango grove. The Buddhist narrative preserves an image of competing ideas and royal curiosity, rather than a kingdom with only one voice.

Pali: rājā māgadho ajātasattu, “King Ajatasattu of Magadha.” This wording appears in the transmitted Samannaphala Sutta. It is shown in modern Roman transcription, not as a surviving inscription or manuscript from the king’s lifetime.

ending.text: Around 321 BCE, Chandragupta overthrew the last Nanda and took Pataliputra. Magadha became the center of the Mauryan state rather than disappearing. The map’s 300 BCE endpoint is a label change, not the destruction of its cities or the end of its people.
